title: The Complexity of Single-Interaction Hamiltonians
abstract: We study the complexity of Local Hamiltonian problems under the restriction that every local term is an unweighted occurrence of the same fixed interaction. In the resulting Single-Interaction Hamiltonian (SIH) model, once the interaction is fixed, the Hamiltonian is specified entirely by its ordered interaction hypergraph.   Our main technical tool is an exact compiler that converts any fixed finite alphabet of local interactions into a single interaction. On a designated auxiliary subspace, the compiled Hamiltonian reproduces the source Hamiltonian exactly, while the complete spectrum below a chosen separation scale is preserved with multiplicity. Combined with a finite-alphabet normalization, this gives a universal polynomial-time reduction from $k$-Local Hamiltonian to SIH$_{3k+3}$ up to a known global energy scale and inverse-polynomial approximation.   Sharper constructions give QMA-completeness of SIH$_3$ and of geometrically local SIH$_8$ with bounded degree and interaction range. In the stoquastic setting, we obtain StoqMA-completeness of Stoq-SIH$_3$ and QMA-completeness of 1-Pinned Stoq-SIH$_4$. We also establish hardness results for uniformly system-size-dependent interactions and derive single-interaction formulations of the Hamiltonian quantum PCP conjecture, frustration-free, exponentially precise, and guided Local Hamiltonian problems. These results show that independently chosen local matrices and independently tunable coupling strengths are not necessary for a broad range of Hamiltonian-complexity phenomena.
summary: This paper analyzes the complexity of quantum Hamiltonians restricted to a Single-Interaction Hamiltonian (SIH) form. Using an exact compiler, the authors show that general Local Hamiltonian problems can be efficiently reduced to SIH models. This establishes that even under severe interaction uniformity, the problem retains significant computational hardness, reaching QMA-completeness for specific cases.
main_problem: The paper investigates the computational complexity of the Local Hamiltonian problem when the local interactions are severely restricted to be unweighted occurrences of a single fixed interaction (Single-Interaction Hamiltonian, SIH).
main_result: It establishes universal polynomial-time reductions from general $k$-Local Hamiltonian problems to SIH models, proving QMA-completeness for specific low-locality SIH variants.
method: The core technique involves an exact compiler that maps an arbitrary finite alphabet of local interactions onto a single interaction using auxiliary qubits, combined with a finite-alphabet normalization procedure.
model_or_system: The model is the Single-Interaction Hamiltonian (SIH), $H_L = \sum_{e \in L} h_e$, where $h$ is a fixed $k$-qubit interaction and $L$ is an ordered hypergraph. Variants include Double-Single-Interaction Hamiltonians (DSIH) and stoquastic versions.
key_observables: The ground state energy and the spectrum below a chosen separation scale are preserved under the reduction.
important_parameters: The locality ($k$), the size of the interaction alphabet ($m$), and the separation scale ($\gamma$) are key parameters determining the complexity and the reduction overhead.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the existence of an exact compiler and a finite-alphabet normalization process, which preserves the low-energy spectrum.
figures_summary: Not specified in the notes; the notes describe theoretical constructions and complexity results rather than figure content.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the SIH model, details the exact compiler tool, presents the universal polynomial-time reduction from $k$-Local Hamiltonian to $	ext{SIH}_{3k+3}$, and concludes with hardness results for various specialized SIH variants (e.g., stoquastic, pinned).
why_interesting: It provides powerful tools to show that even highly constrained physical models (like those restricted to one interaction type) can retain the full computational hardness of general quantum many-body problems.
